report:
Feature 15 is in: if the server is killed at any point, then once it restarts on the same database, each account the note was shared with gets exactly one notice per recorded archiving. `yarn verify` passes, and the work is committed on the current branch as `dfbc4c5` (not pushed).

**Why notices could be lost or doubled before.** Two problems:
- **Lost:** the outbox marked a fact as delivered as soon as the bus took it, but the reaction to it ran later. A crash in between lost the fact.
- **Doubled:** the record of which messages each subscriber had already handled (the inbox) was kept only in memory. After a restart, a fact sent out again reached a subscriber that had already handled it, so the recipient got a second notice.

**The fix**, in the building blocks, so every fact gets it, not just archivings:
- **Delivered means handled.** The bus now reports when every subscriber has handled a message (`IOperation.delivered`), and only then is the outbox entry marked as sent. Until then it stays in the file and goes out again at the next start. A fact that is still being handled isn't sent a second time meanwhile.
- **Each subscriber handles a fact once.** The inbox is now stored with the data (`SqliteInbox`, plus `InMemoryInbox` for in-memory mode). Each reaction checks it and records itself in the same transaction as its own writes, so "handled" and "what handling wrote" are saved together or not at all.
- **The drill.** With `FAULT_DRILL=after-archive`, the server kills itself (`SIGKILL`) right after the first archiving is saved, before doing anything else about it. The code lives only in the composition root (`src/Bootstrap/Fastify/FaultDrill.ts`). The Notes wiring exports the name of the archiving event (`archivingRecorded`) so the drill can spot it.
- **Decision record:** `docs/adr/0008-notices-survive-a-crash.md`, linked from the ADR index. ADR 7's note that a fact could reach a subscriber twice now points to it.

**Tests:**
- `src/Bootstrap/Fastify/crash.e2e.spec.ts` runs the drill and checks the server really was killed. It then restarts three times and checks each recipient has exactly one notice, the owner has none, and a note that was shared but never archived produces no notice.
- `src/Architecture/Infrastructure/Inbox/SqliteInbox.spec.ts` covers the crashes the drill can't reach: one while a reaction is running, and one after a reaction saved but before the outbox marked the fact as sent. With the inbox check switched off, the second test fails, as it should.

**What was unclear, and what I decided:**
- **Changing `src/Architecture`.** `CLAUDE.md` says not to change it for one feature's convenience. I did change it, because its own rules already promise stored-before-sent facts and once-only delivery, and the code didn't keep that promise across a crash. `UnitOfWork` now carries an `inbox`, `IOperation` a `delivered`, and `EventHandler.handle()` takes a subscriber name.
- **What "an archiving that was not recorded" means.** I read it as one whose transaction never committed: it saves nothing, so nobody is told. The end-to-end test only checks this with a note that was never archived; a crash before the commit is covered by the transaction itself rather than by a test.
- **How subscribers are named.** A subscription is named after its event and its handler's class. Renaming a handler class while a fact is waiting to be sent would get that fact handled again. The inbox table is never cleaned up. Both are listed as costs in ADR 8.
- **The archiving person's "operation complete" notice.** If the crash interrupts the archive command itself, the Tracker keeps showing it as `PENDING` and the caller gets no completion notice. That notice goes to the person who archived, not to the people the note was shared with, so I left it alone.
- **Failed reactions.** A reaction that fails is still not retried. Its entry is marked as sent once all subscribers have finished, as before.

Changes sent to the same note at the same moment are now all kept: in memory, in one process on a database file, and across several processes sharing that file. `yarn verify` passes, and the work is committed on the current branch as `679bb34` (not pushed).

**What I found.** The new end-to-end test passed on the old code too, even at 80 shares over three processes, so the danger is in rare timings that test doesn't reliably hit. Reading the code turned up three real ways a change could be lost or refused, and I wrote a narrower spec for each. Two of them run against the old code and fail there: 3 of the 4 new SQLite cases fail, and the in-memory one used to be pinned in the specs as a known limit.
1. **In memory, a reported change could vanish.** Two transactions could overlap, and a rollback put back a copy of the whole store taken when it began. That wiped a share another transaction had already committed and reported done. In-memory transactions now take turns, so a rollback only undoes its own writes. The Tracker's in-memory store is never rolled back, because it is written outside transactions (`InMemoryDataSource({ transactional: false })`).
2. **Across processes, a busy file froze the server and then refused the change.** A process that found the file locked by another one waited synchronously for up to 5 s, serving nothing meanwhile, then failed the command. It now retries every few milliseconds for up to 30 s, and keeps answering requests while it waits.
3. **Writes outside a transaction could be lost.** Those are the Tracker's operation records and the outbox's delivery acknowledgements. If the file was busy, the write was dropped, and an operation could look unfinished forever. It now retries in a transaction of its own.

There are no lost races left to refuse, so the end-to-end test asserts that every change succeeds. Within one process and on the file, each change reads, decides and writes with nobody else's commit in between, so the version check and its three retries should never trigger now; they stay as a backstop. Every process reads what any of them committed straight away. A fact two processes deliver at once still reaches each subscriber once, through the stored inbox from feature 15.

**Tests:**
- **`concurrency.e2e.spec.ts`:** sends twenty shares and an edit of one note at once, in memory, to one process on a file, and spread over three processes on one file. Every change succeeds, every process returns the same note, and every process can report the outcome of an operation another one ran.
- **`SqliteDatabase.spec.ts`:** two connections to one file, standing in for two processes.
- **`InMemoryUnitOfWork.spec.ts`:** the in-memory turn-taking and the store that is never rolled back.

**Decisions to know about:**
- **The building blocks changed again**, this time `InMemoryUnitOfWork`, `InMemoryDataSource` and `SqliteDatabase`, because this is how they keep transactions apart rather than one feature's convenience. It's recorded in `docs/adr/0009-changes-at-the-same-moment.md`, and ADR 7's "revisit when there is more than one process" now points to it.
- **Two existing specs now say the opposite of what they did.** The in-memory spec that pinned "a rollback undoes the other transaction too" now checks that transactions take turns. An event-handler spec that expected a reaction to run beside an open transaction now expects it to wait for that transaction to end, which is what SQLite already did.
- **Cost:** only one write happens at a time on the file. A process that can't get the lock within 30 s refuses the change: `ERROR`, nothing written.

**What was unclear:**
- **"Several processes behind one address."** There's no load balancer in this repository. I took it as several servers on one `DATABASE_PATH`, each on its own port, and didn't add a balancer.
- **Tokens.** As the feature allows, a token from one process doesn't work at another unless they share `TOKEN_SECRET`.

With `NOTIFY_URL` set, every notification a person receives is now also sent to the outside service, again and again until it answers `2xx`, and never after that. `yarn verify` passes (39 suites, 202 tests), and the work is committed on the current branch as `379f8c3` (not pushed).

**How it works:**
- **One stored delivery per notification.** It always carries the same body: `{ id, recipientId, kind, noteId }`, with the `id` that `GET /notifications` lists. It becomes due when the person is told: an archiving at once, a reminder at its moment.
- **Retries.** After a refusal, or no answer within two seconds, the next attempt is due 0.5 s, then 1 s, then 2 s, then every 2.5 s after the attempt ended. So the first retry comes within a second, and attempts start at most about 4.5 s apart, timeout included. Once accepted, the delivery is done for good, and a late answer to it changes nothing.
- **Withdrawn reminders.** A reminder withdrawn before its moment is never sent.
- **Sending.** A loop checks for due deliveries every 200 ms. The HTTP call is made outside any transaction, so a slow service never holds up the application's other writes. Each answer is then recorded in a transaction of its own.
- **Crashes.** Deliveries are stored, so anything not accepted when the server dies goes out on the first round after it starts again. A crash right after a `2xx` but before it was recorded sends the same body once more, which the service tolerates.
- **Without `NOTIFY_URL`,** nothing is scheduled and nothing is sent.
- The design is recorded in `docs/adr/0010-outside-notification-service.md`.

**Tests.** Each rule of the delivery has its own unit test. The end-to-end spec (`outside.e2e.spec.ts`) runs the real server against a fake, unreliable service and checks four things:
- a refusal, then a two-second silence, then acceptance, with the timings above and nothing sent afterwards;
- a reminder that is sent only once its moment has passed;
- a SIGKILL while every attempt is being refused, after which the restarted server sends the same body exactly once and a third start sends nothing;
- that nothing is sent when `NOTIFY_URL` is unset.

**A problem found in my own test setup:** the test helper started servers through the `tsx` wrapper, so a SIGKILL killed the wrapper and left the real server running unseen. In the crash test, that orphan could keep sending and make the test pass for the wrong reason. The helper now starts the server as `node --import tsx`, so the kill reaches the server itself. `crash.e2e.spec.ts` was not affected, because there the server kills itself.

**What was unclear, and what I decided:**
- **Notifications received while `NOTIFY_URL` was unset** are not sent if it is set later. Only those received while it is set go out.
- **Several processes on one database file** may each send the same delivery at the same moment. The service gets the same body twice, which it tolerates because it recognises the id.
- **Retries never stop.** A delivery the service never accepts is tried every 2.5 s indefinitely; there is no point where it gives up.
- **A reminder cancelled very late** (the cancellation is heard after the moment had already come) may already have been sent by then.
- **Building blocks.** Unlike the last two features, `src/Architecture` and `src/SharedKernel` are unchanged. I added `findById` to the notifications repository, some read-only accessors on `Notification`, and an `onStop` hook on the server so the sending loop stops with it.
